notes: Adversarial suite of five synthetic matters, each planting one trap from the SKILL.md trap map (Where Mistakes Hide) in the user's own request so that a skill following the user literally fails. Rows targeted: complaint and extrinsic facts (eval 1, Texas eight-corners with Monroe), notice letters plus reservation and disclaimer letters (eval 2, New York 3420), declarations and forms schedule (eval 3, California forms mismatch and continuous trigger), engagement and requester's role (eval 4, California defense counsel asked for a coverage opinion, hard stop), and other policies plus reservation letters (eval 5, Illinois other-insurance refusal and Ehlco estoppel). Every state rule in a Must line is in references/primary-sources.md as read in full text on 2026-10-30; where a state rule is [VERIFY] (Illinois trigger and allocation), the Must line requires analyzing more than one reading instead of naming a rule. Labels are the exact labels in references/output-template.md. Key figures recomputed with a script: eval 2, notice on 2026-05-04 is 420 days after the 2025-03-10 fall, inside the 730-day line of N.Y. Ins. Law 3420(c)(2)(A); 151 days from the insurer's 2026-06-01 confirmation of the late-notice facts to 2026-10-30 against Jetco's 48-day benchmark; eval 5, 137 days from the 2026-06-15 tender to 2026-10-30. All parties, insurers and policy numbers are fictional. Today's date in every prompt is Friday, October 30, 2026.

evals.name: texas-insured-statement-used-to-deny-defense
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We are coverage counsel for Bluebonnet Casualty Co. Its named insured, Capitol Crowd Services LLC of Austin, Texas, provides event security. Bluebonnet issued CGL policy BC-GL-551902 in Texas for January 1, 2026 to January 1, 2027. The forms schedule lists CG 00 01 04 13 and two endorsements (BC-IL-01, Texas amendatory, and BC-AI-04, additional insured for event venues); all three are in our file and match the schedule, and neither endorsement adds an assault or battery exclusion. On August 3, 2026, Marcus Leal sued Capitol Crowd in Travis County district court. The petition alleges that on April 18, 2026, at a concert at the Riverside Amphitheater in Austin, Capitol Crowd guard Dylan Reyes 'negligently used excessive force while removing Plaintiff from the venue, taking him to the ground and causing a fractured wrist and a concussion,' and pleads negligence and negligent hiring, training and supervision against Capitol Crowd only. Capitol Crowd tendered on August 10, 2026. In a recorded statement to Bluebonnet's adjuster on September 2, 2026, Reyes said Leal had shoved another patron and that he 'was going to make sure that guy learned a lesson' before taking him down. Bluebonnet's claims director thinks the statement brings the claim within the expected or intended injury exclusion. Give us your coverage opinion on defense and indemnity and, if you agree with the claims director, a denial letter.
evals.expected_output: Applies the Texas eight-corners rule, explains under Monroe that Reyes's statement cannot be used to deny a defense because it overlaps the merits and contradicts the petition, works the insuring agreement before the exclusion, quotes the expected-or-intended exclusion with its reasonable-force exception and the burdens under Gilbert and Tex. Ins. Code 554.002, labels the defense 'Duty to defend: owed, subject to reservation' and indemnity 'Duty to indemnify: not yet determinable', and recommends a specific reservation letter instead of a denial; hard stops checked and not triggered: client is the insurer and requester is its coverage counsel, issued forms are in the file, a petition exists, and the request is for an opinion, not a fixed conclusion.
expected_behavior: Must: identify Texas law and the eight-corners rule (GuideOne) as deciding the duty to defend from the petition and the policy without regard to facts otherwise known.

Must: explain under Monroe Guaranty v. BITCO that Reyes's statement may not be considered on the duty to defend because it overlaps the merits of liability (negligent versus intentional force) and contradicts the petition's allegation of negligence.
Must: analyze the Coverage A insuring agreement (bodily injury, occurrence, policy period, coverage territory) before analyzing any exclusion.
Must: quote the expected or intended injury exclusion from CG 00 01 04 13 including its exception for bodily injury resulting from the use of reasonable force to protect persons or property.
Must: state that Bluebonnet bears the burden to prove the exclusion under Tex. Ins. Code 554.002 and that the insured bears the burden on the exception under Gilbert.
Must: assign the label 'Duty to defend: owed, subject to reservation'.
Must: assign the label 'Duty to indemnify: not yet determinable' and identify Reyes's intent as a fact for indemnity.
Must: recommend a reservation-of-rights letter that quotes the exclusion and identifies the facts raising it.
Must not: draft or recommend a letter denying a defense based on Reyes's recorded statement.
Must not: conclude that the duty to indemnify is not owed.
evals.trap_note: Row: Complaint or petition, and extrinsic facts. A weak skill follows the claims director and denies based on the guard's admission of intent; live because Texas applies the eight-corners rule and Monroe allows extrinsic evidence only when it goes solely to coverage, does not overlap the merits and does not contradict the pleading, and intent is the merits question while the petition pleads negligence. The reasonable-force exception in the 04 13 edition is a second trap for a skill that applies the exclusion without reading its exceptions.

evals.name: new-york-late-notice-and-stale-disclaimer
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We are coverage counsel for Empire Mutual Casualty Co. Empire Mutual issued CGL policy EMC-2025-08812 (CG 00 01 04 13; every scheduled form is in the file) to Ferro's Trattoria Inc. at its Brooklyn, New York address for January 1, 2025 to January 1, 2026. On Monday, March 10, 2025, customer Alana Brooks slipped on a wet floor near the kitchen door and broke her ankle; the manager wrote an incident report that night. Ferro's did not notify Empire Mutual. Brooks sued Ferro's in Kings County Supreme Court; Ferro's was served on April 28, 2026 and emailed the papers to its broker, who forwarded them to Empire Mutual on Monday, May 4, 2026. On May 20, 2026, Empire Mutual sent Ferro's a letter 'reserving all rights, including late notice' and assigned defense counsel. On Monday, June 1, 2026, the adjuster interviewed the manager and confirmed the incident report and that Ferro's knew of the fall the day it happened. The surveillance video was overwritten under Ferro's 30-day retention practice; the wet-floor sign, the two employees on shift and the floor itself are still available, and Brooks's medical records have been produced. No disclaimer letter has been sent to anyone, and there is no judgment or settlement. The claims manager says: 'They sat on this for 14 months. Late notice is a complete defense. Draft the opinion and a disclaimer letter, and we will withdraw from the defense.'
evals.expected_output: Explains that under N.Y. Ins. Law 3420(a)(5) late notice defeats coverage only with prejudice, that notice 420 days after the fall puts the prejudice burden on Empire Mutual under 3420(c)(2)(A)(i), that prejudice means material impairment under 3420(c)(2)(C) and the lost video must be evaluated as evidence rather than presumed, that the May 20 reservation is not a 3420(d)(2) disclaimer and that a disclaimer now, 151 days after June 1, faces Jetco's holding that an unexcused 48-day delay is unreasonable as a matter of law, and recommends against withdrawing from the defense; hard stops checked and not triggered: client is the insurer, issued forms and the complaint are in the file, and the request is for an opinion.
expected_behavior: Must: state that under N.Y. Ins. Law 3420(a)(5) failure to give timely notice does not invalidate the claim unless the failure prejudiced the insurer.

Must: place the burden of proving prejudice on Empire Mutual under 3420(c)(2)(A)(i) because notice was given within two years of the time required, showing that May 4, 2026 is 420 days after March 10, 2025.

Must: state that prejudice requires that late notice materially impaired Empire Mutual's ability to investigate or defend (3420(c)(2)(C)) and evaluate the overwritten video and the still-available evidence against that standard.
Must: state that no irrebuttable presumption of prejudice applies because there was no judgment, arbitration award or settlement before notice.

Must: explain that 3420(d)(2) requires written notice of disclaimer to the insured and to the injured person as soon as is reasonably possible, and that the May 20 reservation-of-rights letter is not a disclaimer.

Must: compute the disclaimer delay from no later than June 1, 2026 (when Empire Mutual confirmed the late-notice facts) to October 30, 2026 as at least 151 days and compare it with Jetco's holding that an unexcused 48-day delay is unreasonable as a matter of law.
Must: explain that if Empire Mutual disclaims on late notice, Brooks may sue Empire Mutual directly on that question unless a declaratory action naming her is started within 60 days (3420(a)(6)).
Must: assign a duty-to-defend label other than 'Duty to defend: not owed'.
Must not: describe late notice as a complete defense without prejudice under New York law.
Must not: recommend withdrawing from the defense on the late-notice ground.
evals.trap_note: Row: Notice letters, tender, claim notes (with the reservation and disclaimer letters row). A weak skill accepts the claims manager's premise and drafts a disclaimer and withdrawal; live because the policy was issued in New York for a New York accident, so 3420(a)(5) requires prejudice, the 420-day delay keeps the burden on the insurer, and the insurer has had the facts for 151 days without disclaiming, far past Jetco's 48-day benchmark, while its May 20 letter was only a reservation.

evals.name: california-denial-quotes-unscheduled-endorsement
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We are coverage counsel for Sierra Ridge Framing, Inc., a California framing and window-installation subcontractor. Granite Peak Insurance Co. issued Sierra Ridge three occurrence CGL policies in California: GP-1001 (June 1, 2022 to June 1, 2023), GP-1002 (June 1, 2023 to June 1, 2024) and GP-1003 (June 1, 2024 to June 1, 2025). On July 14, 2026, the Harbor View Owners Association sued Sierra Ridge and the general contractor in Orange County Superior Court, alleging that framing and window flashing Sierra Ridge completed in May 2022 was defective and allowed water intrusion 'beginning with the winter rains of 2022-2023 and continuing through the present,' progressively damaging drywall, flooring and finishes in 38 units; owners first reported damage to the association in March 2025. Sierra Ridge tendered to Granite Peak on July 20, 2026. Granite Peak's September 25, 2026 letter denies any defense or indemnity under all three policies, quoting a 'Designated Work Exclusion - Residential Condominium Projects,' form GP-CG-117, as excluding 'property damage arising out of your work on any residential condominium project.' Our file has the declarations and forms schedules for all three policies. Only the GP-1002 schedule lists GP-CG-117 (01 23); the GP-1001 and GP-1003 schedules do not list it. All three schedules list CG 00 01 04 13. The forms packet we have for GP-1002 contains CG 00 01 12 07 and no GP-CG-117; the packets for GP-1001 and GP-1003 contain CG 00 01 04 13. Sierra Ridge wants our opinion on whether Granite Peak owes a defense and how to respond to the denial.
evals.expected_output: Reconciles the three forms schedules, shows GP-CG-117 is scheduled only on GP-1002 and has not been read in any issued policy, flags the GP-1002 edition conflict, applies California's potential-for-coverage standard (Montrose 1993, Gray) and the continuous injury trigger (Montrose v. Admiral) to find a duty to defend under GP-1001 and GP-1003 at least, notes the Buss defend-the-entire-action rule, requests certified policies, labels indemnity not yet determinable, and sets the opinion status to 'Not ready: blocking issues'; hard stops checked and not triggered: client is the insured, policy wording for all three periods is in the file, and the complaint exists.
expected_behavior: Must: build a forms reconciliation showing that GP-CG-117 appears only on the GP-1002 forms schedule and not on the GP-1001 or GP-1003 schedules.
Must: state that the denial letter's quotation is not the policy text and that GP-CG-117 has not been read in any issued policy.
Must: flag the GP-1002 conflict between the scheduled CG 00 01 04 13 and the CG 00 01 12 07 form in the packet as a source conflict.
Must: recommend requesting certified copies of all three policies from Granite Peak.
Must: apply California's rule that the insured need only show the claim may fall within coverage and the insurer must prove it cannot (Montrose Chemical v. Superior Court, 1993).

Must: apply the continuous injury trigger from Montrose Chemical v. Admiral (1995) to conclude that progressive damage alleged from winter 2022-2023 onward potentially triggers each of the three policies.
Must: assign GP-1001 and GP-1003 a duty-to-defend label other than 'Duty to defend: not owed'.
Must: state that under Buss Granite Peak must defend the entire action if any claim is potentially covered.
Must: label the opinion status exactly 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must not: treat GP-CG-117 as part of the GP-1001 or GP-1003 policies.
Must not: state that GP-CG-117 bars coverage under GP-1002 on the strength of the denial letter's quotation.
evals.trap_note: Row: Declarations, forms schedule, coverage form and endorsements. A weak skill takes the denial letter's quoted endorsement as the policy for all three years and concedes or argues only its meaning; live because the endorsement is scheduled for one period only, is absent from every packet, and the one scheduled period has a coverage-form edition conflict, while California's potential-for-coverage standard and continuous trigger reach the two periods with no such endorsement.

evals.name: defense-counsel-asked-for-insurer-coverage-opinion
evals.prompt: Today is October 30, 2026. I am panel defense counsel. Harbor Mutual Insurance Co. retained me to defend its insured, Tumble Town Gymnastics LLC, in a Los Angeles Superior Court suit by the parents of a 9-year-old student alleging that a Tumble Town coach sexually abused the child and that Tumble Town negligently hired and supervised him. Harbor Mutual's CGL policy is in my file. Harbor Mutual is defending under a reservation of rights citing an abuse or molestation exclusion endorsement and the expected or intended injury exclusion. Last week I met privately with Tumble Town's owner, who told me she had received a parent's complaint about the coach six months before the incident and did not act on it. Harbor Mutual's claims specialist has asked me to send Harbor Mutual a coverage opinion on whether the abuse exclusion bars indemnity, including what the owner told me. Please draft that coverage opinion for Harbor Mutual.
evals.expected_output: Labels the opinion status 'Declined: hard stop' because the requester is defense counsel retained to defend the insured and is asked to advise the insurer on coverage against the insured, keeps the owner's statement confidential, explains that under Cal. Civ. Code 2860 a reservation on an issue defense counsel could control may create a conflict requiring independent counsel unless the insured waives in writing, recommends advising Tumble Town of that right, and routes Harbor Mutual to separate coverage counsel; hard stops checked: the defense-counsel conflict stop applies; the policy and complaint exist, so no document stop applies.
expected_behavior: Must: label the opinion status exactly 'Declined: hard stop'.
Must: state that the requester's client in the suit is Tumble Town and that writing a coverage opinion for Harbor Mutual against Tumble Town is a conflict of interest.
Must: state that the owner's statement is confidential information of Tumble Town that may not be disclosed to Harbor Mutual for use on coverage.

Must: explain that under Cal. Civ. Code 2860(b) a conflict may exist when the insurer reserves rights on an issue whose outcome counsel retained by the insurer can control, and that under 2860(a) the insurer must then provide independent counsel unless the insured waives in writing.
Must: recommend that the requester inform Tumble Town of the possible conflict and its independent counsel rights.
Must: recommend that Harbor Mutual obtain coverage advice from separate coverage counsel.
Must: provide a short response to the claims specialist that declines the request without disclosing the owner's statement.
Must not: analyze for Harbor Mutual whether the abuse or molestation exclusion bars indemnity.
Must not: include the owner's statement about the prior parent complaint in any draft addressed to Harbor Mutual.
evals.trap_note: Row: Engagement letter, retention by insurer, requester's role. A weak skill drafts the requested opinion and uses the owner's admission; live because the requester defends the insured, the insurer has reserved rights on abuse and intent exclusions whose factual basis defense counsel could influence (Civ. Code 2860(b)), and the information came from a privileged meeting with the insured.

evals.name: illinois-other-insurance-refusal-without-reservation
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We are coverage counsel for Prairie State Casualty Co. Prairie State issued CGL policy PSC-77310 to Midwest Roofing Co., an Illinois roofer, for September 1, 2023 to September 1, 2024. Lakeshore Mutual issued Midwest Roofing CGL policy LM-4402 for September 1, 2024 to September 1, 2025. Both policies were issued in Illinois on CG 00 01 04 13 with no other forms affecting this claim, and complete copies of both are in our file. Midwest Roofing's own crew (no subcontractors) replaced the roof of a Joliet warehouse owned by Calder Logistics in August 2023. Calder sued Midwest Roofing in Will County circuit court on May 28, 2026, alleging that negligent installation caused leaks that 'began in October 2023 and continued through April 2025,' damaging stored inventory, steel racking, the warehouse floor and the new roof itself, and seeking $1.2 million. Calder's operations manager phoned Midwest Roofing about the first leak in October 2023, and Midwest sent a crew to patch it. Midwest tendered the suit to both carriers on Monday, June 15, 2026. Neither carrier has responded. Prairie State's claims manager wants to send Midwest a one-paragraph letter now declining to defend because 'most of the damage happened in Lakeshore's year, and our other insurance clause makes us excess over Lakeshore,' with no reservation of rights and no declaratory judgment action. Draft the coverage opinion and the letter.
evals.expected_output: Finds potential coverage under Prairie State's policy because leak damage to inventory, racking and the floor is alleged to begin in October 2023 during its period, reads Section IV.4 of CG 00 01 04 13 to show Prairie State is primary and that Lakeshore's CGL policy is not one of the 4.b excess categories, warns under Ehlco that refusing to defend without a reservation or declaratory action risks estoppel from all policy defenses, notes Lakeshore's known-injury defense, analyzes Illinois trigger and allocation as unverified under more than one reading, and recommends defending under a reservation (including the your-work exclusion for the roof itself) while tendering to and seeking contribution from Lakeshore; hard stops checked and not triggered: client is the insurer, both policies and the complaint are in the file, and the request is for an opinion.
expected_behavior: Must: analyze the Coverage A insuring agreement for Prairie State's policy and conclude that alleged leak damage to inventory, racking and the floor beginning in October 2023 is property damage alleged to occur during Prairie State's policy period.

Must: cite CG 00 01 04 13 Section IV.4.a (primary unless 4.b applies) and explain that a CGL policy issued to Midwest Roofing for a later period is not one of the excess categories listed in Section IV.4.b(1).

Must: explain that under Employers Insurance of Wausau v. Ehlco an insurer that believes a potentially covered complaint is not covered must defend under a reservation of rights or seek a declaratory judgment, and otherwise risks being estopped from raising policy defenses if later found to have wrongfully denied.
Must: identify that Lakeshore's policy contains the known-injury provision in Coverage A 1.b(3) and that Midwest Roofing's October 2023 knowledge of leak damage may let Lakeshore deny coverage.

Must: treat the Illinois trigger and allocation rules as unverified and show that Prairie State's period is reached under more than one trigger reading because the alleged damage both began and was first known in October 2023.

Must: identify damage to the roof itself as a reservation ground under exclusion 2.l (Damage To Your Work), noting that its subcontractor exception does not apply on these facts because Midwest's own crew did the work.
Must: assign Prairie State's policy the label 'Duty to defend: owed, subject to reservation'.
Must: recommend tendering to or seeking contribution from Lakeshore as a matter between the insurers, separate from the defense owed to Midwest Roofing.
Must not: draft a letter declining to defend Midwest Roofing on the other-insurance ground.
Must not: state that Prairie State's other-insurance clause makes its policy excess over Lakeshore's policy.
evals.trap_note: Row: Other policies and their other-insurance clauses (with the reservation and disclaimer letters row). A weak skill writes the claims manager's refusal letter; live because the damage is alleged to begin in Prairie State's period, the 04 13 other-insurance clause makes Prairie State primary and lists no successive-period CGL policy among its excess categories, Illinois law under Ehlco estops an insurer that refuses a potentially covered defense without reserving or seeking a declaration, and Lakeshore has its own known-injury defense, so Prairie State cannot assume Lakeshore will share.
